chunks: What an EEPROM is. The question: What is an EEPROM?
EEPROM is memory that keeps its data without power, and that you can erase and rewrite electrically one byte at a time.
It usually comes as a small chip that you talk to over a serial bus (a few shared wires that carry data one bit at a time) such as I2C or SPI.
It is used for small things that change rarely, such as calibration values, a serial number, or user settings.
Think of a guest book where you can erase and rewrite a single line without touching the others.
A flash memory is more like a book where you must tear out and replace a whole page to change one word. The guest book is handy for small edits.
But each erase scuffs the paper, so a line can be rewritten only so many times. Each write also keeps the pen busy for a few milliseconds.
A page write has two phases. The bus transaction is short, then the chip goes busy for t WC and NACKs its address.
Polling until the first ACK finishes the write as early as possible, instead of waiting a fixed worst-case delay.
Non-volatile: ("What non-volatile memory means"): keeps its contents when power is removed.
ROM family: ("What ROM is"): EEPROM is the ROM version that can be electrically erased and rewritten.
Write cycle time: a few milliseconds during which the chip is busy storing and ignores the bus. Page write: writing several bytes in one write cycle.
The bytes must stay inside one page, or the address wraps around. Endurance: how many times a byte can be rewritten before it may fail.
You store one calibration byte. The microcontroller sends the chip's address, the byte's address, and the value over I2C.
Then the chip is busy for a few milliseconds, so you keep asking until it answers again. Reading it back later is fast.
If a part is rated for 1 million writes and you rewrite one byte every second, it wears out in about 11. 6 days. So write only when the value changes. That is the whole idea.
"An EEPROM is non-volatile memory you can erase and rewrite electrically, one byte or small page at a time.
Cells are floating-gate transistors written by tunnelling, so data lasts decades without power but wears out after roughly 10^5 to 10^6 writes.
Typically it's a small I2C or SPI chip for calibration or settings. Writes take a few milliseconds, and you poll for completion.
For big or frequently changing data, use flash or FRAM instead."
